summary: Teach genetic mutation (ages 12–14) as a random change in DNA base sequence that can alter the protein a gene codes for, arising from mutagens (ionising/UV radiation, certain chemicals) and spontaneous DNA-copying errors. The load-bearing ideas: most mutations are neutral, some harmful, a few beneficial in a given environment; mutation is random with respect to need; and mutation is the ultimate source of heritable variation that natural selection then sorts. In sexually reproducing animals, only mutations in the germ line (cells that make gametes) are passed to offspring and matter for evolution; in single-celled organisms such as bacteria, any mutation is passed on when the cell divides. The central activity lets learners generate the effect distribution themselves and feed a beneficial variant into a selection round, correcting the common 'directed mutation' and 'all mutations are harmful' errors.
misconceptions: Believing mutations happen because an organism needs them (directed/adaptive mutation) rather than randomly.
Thinking all mutations are harmful or produce dramatic monstrosities, missing that most are neutral.
Assuming mutations are always visible or always change the organism, ignoring silent/non-coding changes.
Confusing body-cell (somatic) mutations, which aren't inherited, with heritable gamete mutations relevant to evolution.
Thinking mutation and natural selection are the same thing, rather than mutation supplying variation that selection then acts on.
Believing beneficial or harmful is absolute, rather than dependent on the current environment.

activities.title: Flip a base, watch the consequence
steps: Start with a short DNA stretch that includes a gene for a simple working protein (and its trait) plus some non-coding DNA, as real genomes do.
Trigger a randomiser that flips one base at random — standing in for a stray bit of radiation or a copying slip — so you cannot choose which base changes or aim for a 'good' result.

Observe how each flip resolves: NEUTRAL (the protein is unchanged or still works — a silent or non-coding change), HARMFUL (the protein breaks and the organism suffers), or BENEFICIAL (the protein happens to work better in the current environment).
Repeat many random flips and build a tally/bar of outcomes to see the overall distribution emerge.
Raise a 'mutagen dose' control to increase the mutation rate and watch more changes appear; in this model the proportion that are beneficial does not rise with the rate.
Take one lucky beneficial variant into a quick selection round where the better-fitting organisms survive and reproduce.
State in your own words where new variation comes from and what selection does with it.
activities.insight: Mutation is a random change to the DNA sequence: across many random changes most are neutral, some harmful, and a few beneficial in the current environment. You can never aim for a beneficial mutation — change is random with respect to need — yet those rare beneficial changes are the raw material that natural selection keeps. Mutation supplies variation; selection is the non-random filter.

activities.title: Question a geneticist: did it mutate because it needed to?
steps: Pose or respond to challenge questions with a geneticist in role, e.g. 'Did the bacterium mutate BECAUSE it needed resistance?' and 'If mutations are usually harmful, how can they drive evolution?'
Explain in discussion that resistance mutations arise at random before or regardless of the antibiotic, and the antibiotic only selects among what is already there.
Work through what would happen to a resistant mutant that arose when no antibiotic was present.
Summarise why 'random origin' and 'non-random selection' are two separate steps.
activities.insight: Mutations arise randomly and independently of what the organism needs; the environment does not create the useful change, it selects among changes that already exist. Even when most mutations are harmful, the rare beneficial ones supply the variation selection acts on.

activities.title: Sort the effects and name the causes
steps: Categorise example mutations by effect: neutral, harmful, or beneficial, explaining your reasoning for each.
Match causes of mutation — UV/ionising radiation and certain chemicals (mutagens), plus spontaneous DNA-copying errors — to short descriptions of how each produces a change.

Choose the correct account of why an antibiotic-resistant strain appears, rejecting the option 'the bacteria mutated because they needed to survive' in favour of 'random mutation already present, then selection'.
Explain whether a mutation in a body cell or a gamete matters for evolution, and why.
activities.insight: Learners can discriminate the three effect categories, connect real causes (external mutagens AND spontaneous copying errors) to physical mechanisms, and distinguish heritable gamete mutations from somatic ones.

activities.title: Reference map: DNA → gene → protein → mutation outcomes
steps: Study an annotated base sequence and reveal example mutations that show neutral, harmful, and beneficial outcomes along with the mechanism for each.
Read a callout explaining causes of mutation — mutagens (UV/ionising radiation, chemicals) and spontaneous copying errors — and how each damages or alters DNA.
Use the vocabulary (DNA sequence, base, gene, protein, mutagen, neutral/harmful/beneficial) to describe one worked example before moving to the hands-on activity.
activities.insight: Learners gain the vocabulary and the three effect categories and can see how a single base change maps to a protein and trait outcome.

checkQuestion: Bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic, and soon a resistant strain appears. A student says: 'The antibiotic made the bacteria mutate so they could survive.' Is that the right way to describe how the resistance arose? Explain what actually happened.
checkAnswer: No. Mutations happen randomly, independently of what the bacteria 'need'. By chance a few bacteria already carried a resistance mutation before (or regardless of) the antibiotic; the antibiotic did not create the mutation — it selected for it, killing the non-resistant bacteria and letting the resistant ones survive and reproduce. The mutation is random; the selection is not.
